The Wikimedia terms, section 7 allow licensed text reuse with attribution, require preservation of applicable additional attribution notices, and require adapted text to retain CC BY-SA terms and identify modifications. The extracted dates match all 13 senior Series spans in the World Climbing January calendar announcement. Source labels are preserved: Wikipedia calls the Spanish stop Madrid, while the announcement calls its host municipality Alcobendas. No exact arena is invented. The source's Guiyang September 11–13 inclusive span also matches the official event page. The previous research found a disagreement over individual Speed rounds on September 11 versus 12 in a separate generated feed. No such rounds, timestamps or inferred durations are included here; the stop span is unaffected.

The dates range from May 1–3 at Keqiao to October 23–25 at Santiago. IDs include season and stop identity, so future date corrections do not create new events. This scope excludes youth, para, continental events, Games, a separate Nations Grand Finale, and a nonexistent 2026 senior World Championship. It does not claim to cover every event organized by World Climbing.

All nine remaining race dates, September 13 through November 8, agree with NASCAR's August 5 television-calendar article. That article still calls the October 11 track the Charlotte Roval. The venue's September 10 notice confirms the race is on the oval and calls it Bank of America 400. The pinned Wikipedia source already has that corrected name and plain Charlotte Motor Speedway venue, which are retained. This is a resolved source-age disagreement, not a reason to change the supported October 11 race date.

- Nashville is July 20, not the original July 19. INDYCAR's postponement notice confirms the move after rain. - Milwaukee round 16 is August 29–30, representing one interrupted race. INDYCAR's resumption notice confirms that the first race began Saturday and continued Sunday. Round 17 remains a separate August 30 race. The remaining dates were reviewed against the pinned table, with the current official schedule used as a secondary sanity check; no exhaustive independent audit of all race sponsor titles was performed. No practice, qualifying, warmup, support-series or exact clocks are published.

Both information sheets contain inconsistent offset headings: Salt Lake says local time UTC+8; Santiago says local time UTC+2. These are not used as offsets. The interpretation as venue local wall clocks follows the sheets' explicit local-time label and the Santiago organizer's explicit offset, with conversion through IANA America/Denver (MDT, UTC−06:00 on October 16–18) and America/Santiago (UTC−03:00 on October 23–25). This is a documented correction to the headings, not a claim that the organizers corrected their PDFs. IANA North America rules and South America rules provide the zone rules; Chile's 2026 Decree 98 extends the seasonal regime from September 2026.

Unknown clocks have null UTC/local/zone fields and a visible explanation, never a synthetic midnight. The existing UI converts agreed instants to the visitor's timezone; Salt Lake's 19:00 finals therefore appear on October 18 and 19 in UTC. Unknown clocks stay on the venue calendar date.

The two whole-stop rows are replaced by 16 gender/discipline/round rows; 11 earlier stops remain inclusive date-only spans. The resulting calendar has 27 climbing records representing the same 13 stops. Each actually scheduled combination of women/men, discipline and round has its own pill; no separate Speed semi-final is invented inside the finals session. Discipline tags (Boulder, Lead, Speed) use the existing tag representation and appear alongside discipline names in session titles. Earlier stops' tags come from their existing pinned Wikipedia extraction, without a new source or inferred disciplines.

Session starts are not first-athlete, first-race, broadcast or warmup clocks. No end times, durations, practice, isolation, medals or separate gender clocks for combined sessions are inferred. Four round records carry start_time_scope: "shared_session": the two Speed finals and two Lead semi-finals. Their UTC/local timestamps represent the agreed shared session start, and the UI says Session starts … in previews, details and agendas. Their notes explicitly say the individual gender start is not separately published. There are seven individual starts, four shared-session markers and five unknown clocks across 16 round records.
